notes.text: About to take, &c. — It is supposed, (tho' not expressly revealed) that Elijah flourished about twenty years, before he was translated, body and soul, to heaven, only undergoing such a change, as was necessary to qualify him for being an inhabitant in that world of Spirits. By translating him, God gave in that dark and degenerate age, a very sensible proof of another life, together with a type of the ascension of Christ, and the opening of the kingdom of heaven to all believers.

Tarry here — This he desires, either,

1. That being left alone, he might better prepare himself for his great change. Or,

2. Out of indulgence to Elisha, that he might not be overwhelmed with grief at so sad a sight. Or,

3. That he might try his love, and whet his desire to accompany him; it being highly convenient for God's honour, that there should be witnesses of so glorious a translation. To Beth-el - Which was truth, tho' not the whole truth: for he was to go a far longer journey. But he was first to go to Beth-el, as also to Jericho, to the schools of the prophets there, that he might comfort, and strengthen their hearts in God's work, and give them his dying counsels.

And said — This was revealed to some of the sons of the prophets, and by them to the whole college. In the kingdom of Judah they had priest and Levites, and the temple service. The want of these in the kingdom of Israel, God graciously made up by these colleges, where men were trained up and employed, in the exercises of religion, and whither good people resorted, to solemnize the appointed feasts, with prayer and hearing, tho' they had not conveniencies for sacrifice. From thy head - Hebrew. from above thy head: which phrase may respect, either, the manner of sitting in schools, where the scholar sat at his master's feet. Or, the manner of Elijah's translation, which was to be by a power sent from heaven, to take him up thither. Hold you your peace - Do not aggravate my grief, nor divert me with any unseasonable discourses. He speaks as one that was himself, and would have them calm and sedate, and with awful silence waiting the event.

To view — To observe this great event, Elijah's translation to heaven, which they expected every moment: and whereof they desired to be spectators, not to satisfy their own curiosity, but that they might be witnesses of it to others.

Smote the waters — These waters of old yielded to the ark, now to the prophet's mantle; which to those that wanted the ark, was an equivalent token of God's presence. When God will take his children to himself, death is the Jordan, which they must pass through. And they find a way thro' it, a safe and comfortable way. The death of Christ has divided those waters, that the ransomed of the Lord may pass over.

A double portion — Or, rather double to what the rest of the sons of the prophets receive at thy request. He alludes to the double portion of the first-born, Deut. xxi, 17. But though Elisha desired no more, yet God gave him more than he desired or expected; and he seems to have had a greater portion of the gifts of God's Spirit, than even Elijah had.

A hard thing — A rare and singular blessing, which I cannot promise thee, which only God can give; and he gives it only when, and to whom he pleaseth. If thou seest - This sign he proposed, not without the direction of God's Spirit, that hereby he might engage him more earnestly to wait, and more fervently to pray for this mercy.

A chariot of fire — In this form the angels appeared. The souls of all the faithful, are carried by an invisible guard of angels, into the bosom of Abraham. But Elijah being to carry his body with him, this heavenly guard appeared visibly: Not in an human shape, tho' so they might have born him in their arms, but in the form of a chariot and horses, that he may ride in state, may ride in triumph, like a prince, like a conqueror. See the readiness of the angels to do the will of God, even in the meanest services for the heirs of salvation! Thus he who had burned with holy zeal for God and his honour, was now conveyed in fire into his immediate presence.

My father — So he calls him for his fatherly affection to him, and for his fatherly authority which he had over him, in which respect the scholars of the prophets are called their sons. He saw his own condition like that of a fatherless child, and laments it accordingly. The chariot, &c. - Who by thy example, and counsels, and prayers, and power with God, didst more for the defense and preservation of Israel than all their chariots and horses. The expression alludes to the form of chariots and horses which he had seen.

glossa.text: *It came to pass. ((RAB. in lib. Reg., t. III.))* A whirlwind, that is, a most violent wind, etc., *as far as* The Lord was taken up, neither begetting by intercourse nor begotten.

*Let it be in.* Elias was mightily strong in the spirit of prophecy and in the working of miracles, the twofold grace, therefore, which Elisaeus knew to flourish in his master, he asked to be granted to himself. Whence it is plain that he asked not to be a disciple above his master. ((RAB.)) Having received from the Lord confidence in asking, the Church asks for the Spirit of Christ, and because she has need of the remission of sins, of which Christ had no need, and of the gift of the virtues which Christ out of his fullness bestows through the Holy Spirit, *who ascending on high, led captivity captive, gave gifts to men ((Ephes. IV))*, to those, namely, who place their hope in him. Hence it is that he says:

*If thou shalt see.* That is, if thou shalt open the eyes of faith, and shalt faithfully believe, together with the passion and the resurrection, my ascension also, thou shalt obtain the effect of thy petition.

notes.text: Called — All the inhabitants of the earth, from one end to the other: whom he here summons to be witnesses of his proceedings in this solemn judgment, between him and his people, which is here poetically represented. For here is a tribunal erected, the judge coming to it, the witnesses and delinquents summoned, and at last the sentence given.

Zion — The place where he was supposed to reside, and where he would now sit in judgment. The perfection - The most amiable place of the whole world, because, of the presence and worship, and blessing of God. Shined - Hath manifested himself in a glorious manner.

Our God — The prophet speaks this in the persons of the worshippers of God. Though he be our God, yet he will come to execute judgment upon us. Cease - Or delay to sit in judgment. Tempestuous - This is a farther description of that terrible majesty, wherewith God would clothe himself when he came to his tribunal.
Call — To the inhabitants of them, all angels and men, whom he calls in for witnesses of the equity of his proceedings.

Gather — O ye angels, summon and fetch them to my tribunal. Which is poetically spoken, to continue the metaphor, and representation of the judgment. My saints - The Israelites, whom God had chosen and separated them from all the nations of the earth, to be an holy and peculiar people to himself, and they also had solemnly devoted themselves to God; all which aggravated their apostacy. Those - Who have entered into covenant with me, and have ratified that covenant by sacrifice. This seems to be added, to acquaint them with the proper nature, use and end of sacrifices, which were principally appointed to be signs and seals of the covenant made between God and his people; and consequently to convince them of their great mistake in trusting to their outward sacrifices, when they neglected the very life and soul of them, which was the keeping of their covenant with God.

Declare — God will convince the people of his righteousness, and of their own wickedness, by thunders and lightnings, and storms, or other dreadful signs wrought by him in the heavens. Himself - In his own person. God will not now reprove them, by his priests or prophets, but in an extraordinary manner from heaven.

glossa.text: *A psalm of Asaph.* ((HIER.)) *Asaph,* in Latin a congregation; in Greek, a synagogue, which here speaks as faithful, which awaits Christ, through which the unbelieving Jews are the more confuted. ((CASS.)) *Asaph,* about to bring in the voice of God concerning the change of the sacrifices, first treats of both comings, by the first inviting, by the second terrifying. *God of gods.* ((CASS.)) Lest anyone think meanly of the incarnation, etc., *as far as* by way of appellation, as the false gods, Jupiter, Venus. *He hath spoken, and hath called the earth.* ((AUG.)) By himself, by heralds. *From the rising of the sun unto the going down.* ((CASS.)) As if he should say, etc., *as far as: the law shall come forth from Sion, and the Word of the Lord from Jerusalem.*
*Out of Sion, the loveliness of his beauty,* etc. ((AUG.)) The comeliness of the Gospel began, etc., *as far as* that they might be witnesses in Jerusalem and in the whole earth.

*Fire shall blaze in his sight and round about him. ((Ibid.))* It shall go before him; let punishment therefore terrify those whom rewards do not invite, etc., *as far as* it shall accompany the wicked to hell. *A mighty tempest. He shall call heaven from above, and the earth.* *Tempesta* ((CASS.)) Not a wind, etc., *as far as* first he called all in common, then he shall call that he may separate. *To judge his people.* ((AUG.)) First he called the mingled from the rising of the sun unto the going down, but then that he may separate.

*Gather ye together his saints unto him. ((Ibid.))* The Prophet seeing things to come, etc., *as far as* it is said of the wicked, *of whom he hath not filled his hand. Who set his covenant above sacrifices. ((Ibid.))*. The New Testament above the Old, etc., *as far as* who hold the works of charity of more worth than the sacrifices of cattle.

*And the heavens shall declare his justice,* etc. ((Ibid.)) Already the heavens have declared to us this justice of God, etc., *as far as* and if now things are mingled, because *God is a just judge.*

notes.text: But if our gospel also — As well as the law of Moses.

The God of this world — What a sublime and horrible description of Satan! He is indeed the God of all that believe not, and works in them with inconceivable energy. Hath blinded - Not only veiled, the eye of their understanding. Illumination - Is properly the reflection or propagation of light, from those who are already enlightened, to others. Who is the image of God - Hence also we may understand how great is the glory of Christ. He that sees the Son, sees the Father in the face of Christ. The Son exactly exhibits the Father to us.

For — The fault is not in us, neither in the doctrine they hear from us. We preach not ourselves - As able either to enlighten, or pardon, or sanctify you. But Jesus Christ - As your only wisdom, righteousness, sanctification. And ourselves your servants - Ready to do the meanest offices. For Jesus' sake - Not for honour, interest, or pleasure.

For God hath shined in our hearts — The hearts of all those whom the God of this world no longer blinds. God who is himself our light; not only the author of light, but also the fountain of it. To enlighten us with the knowledge of the glory of God - Of his glorious love, and of his glorious image. In the face of Jesus Christ - Which reflects his glory in another manner than the face of Moses did.

glossa.text:
*In whom.* The order of the words can be such: In whom that perish, the true and just God hath blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this world.

*The god of this world.* That is, God who not only rules the good, but also casts down the evil according to their desert, giving them what they will, that is, that they should not believe: which malice does not do, but justice. Or, the god of this world is pride or gluttony, or the devil the prince of the world, who over worldly men bears rule.

*For we preach not ourselves.* As if he should say: I speak well unto the glory of Christ, or: We have commended ourselves before God in the manifestation of the truth, and we do other such things; and this for Christ's sake.

*Light to shine.* Which was in the separation of the elements. For darkness began from the time when the confused mass of heaven and earth began to be: afterwards, the light being added, which was done; it is rendered better. In which the disposition of the man who makes progress is signified, whence *you were heretofore darkness, but now light in the Lord ((Ephes. V))*. *In the face of Jesus.* It has this sense: Since the divine nature falls not under sight, it is beheld, so far as is permitted, through the assumed humanity that shines back with the divine light and sends forth lightnings. And hence it is also manifest that God did not send in unbelief, who has abundantly furnished to all the splendour of the light that gives understanding: but they indeed loved unbelief, while he, when they would not look, did not furnish them the ray. *Of the knowledge of the brightness.* The knowledge of the glory of God is that whereby we know that there is a light by which our darkness is enlightened.

notes.text: By themselves — That is, separate from the multitude: Apart - From the other apostles: and was transfigured - The Greek word seems to refer to the form of God, and the form of a servant, {mentioned by St. Paul, Phil. ii, 6, 7} and may intimate, that the Divine rays, which the indwelling God let out on this occasion, made the glorious change from one of these forms into the other. Matt. xvii, 1; Luke ix, 28.
White as snow, such as no fuller can whiten — Such as could not be equalled either by nature or art.
Elijah — Whom they expected: Moses, whom they did not.

There came a (bright, luminous) cloud, overshadowing them — This seems to have been such a cloud of glory as accompanied Israel in the wilderness, which, as the Jewish writers observe, departed at the death of Moses. But it now appeared again, in honour of our Lord, as the great Prophet of the Church, who was prefigured by Moses. Hear ye him - Even preferably to Moses and Elijah.

glossa.text: *And his garments.* The garments of the Lord are the saints. Whence: *You who have been baptized in Christ have put on Christ ((Gal. III))*. These, while the Lord remained in the world, seemed despised; but when he sought the mountain they shine again with a new whiteness. *Because now indeed we are the sons of God, but it hath not yet appeared what we shall be. When therefore he shall appear, we shall be like to him, because we shall see him as he is ((I Joan. III))*. Whence it is subjoined.

*And there appeared,* etc. Moses, a holy man dead, and Elias, caught up alive into heaven, seen in majesty with the Lord (as Luke says), signify the glory of all the saints to come in him: who at the time of judgment shall be found either alive in the flesh or dead.

*Elias with. ((BEDA.))* The lawgiver and the chief of the prophets appear: they speak with the Lord living in the flesh, showing that he is the one whom the law and the prophets promised; not in the lowest places, but on the mountain with him, because they who pass beyond earthly desires in mind perceive that the majesty of Holy Scripture, which has been fulfilled in the Lord, is unfolded.

*Rabbi.* Although astonished, etc., *as far as* having one tabernacle, that is, the Church of God. *It is good.* Much better therefore is it to be among the choirs of the saints, and to enjoy the vision of the Godhead: if the humanity of Christ transfigured so delights, and the company of two shown for a moment.

*A cloud overshadowing.* Whence, because he sought a material tabernacle, he received the shade of a cloud, that he might learn that in the resurrection the saints are to be protected, not by the covering of houses, but by the Holy Spirit. *This is.* As if he said: This is truly he whom that Moses promised you, etc., *as far as* and it shall be enlightened by the same grace, and shall be protected for ever.

*And immediately. ((BEDA.))* When the voice came over the Son of man, he alone was found. Because when he shall have manifested himself to the elect, God will be all in all: nay rather, he himself with his own, one Christ throughout all, that is, the head with the body, shall shine forth; whence: *No man hath ascended into heaven, but he that descended from heaven, the Son of man, who is in heaven ((Joan. III))*.

*He charged them.* He wills not that the glory of the kingdom to come and of the triumph which he had shown on the mountain be publicly preached: lest both it should be past belief for its greatness, and, after so great a glory, the cross that followed should make a scandal among untaught minds.

*They kept the word. ((HIER.))* That is, when death shall have been swallowed up in victory, the former things shall not be in memory, when the Lord shall have taken away the filth of the daughter of Sion, wiping away every tear from the eyes of the saints.

Holy Spirit You Are Welcome Here

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)
Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Make the heart of this people fat. Make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes; lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their heart, and turn again, and be healed.”
echoes.note: The 'god of this world has blinded the minds' so they cannot see the light recasts Isaiah's hardening commission, where eyes are made blind 'lest they see.' High recurrence in Paul (Rom 11:8) and strong coherence with the veiling theme of ch. 3 support a deliberate allusion.

echoes.text: God said, “Let us make man in our image, after our likeness: and let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the birds of the sky, and over the livestock, and over all the earth, and over every creeping thing that creeps on the earth.”
echoes.note: Calling Christ 'the image of God' reads the creation of humanity in God's image figurally, with Christ as the true eikon. The pairing of image (4:4) and the creation of light (4:6) keys the whole pericope to Genesis 1, making this a deliberate new-creation typology.

echoes.text: God said, “Let there be light,” and there was light.
echoes.note: 'God who said, Light will shine out of darkness' rewords the creation fiat, presenting conversion as a new act of creation in the heart. The volume is high (clear verbal evocation of the fiat lux) and coherent with the Genesis 1 image motif of 4:4.

echoes.text: But Yahweh has not given you a heart to know, eyes to see, and ears to hear, to this day.
echoes.note: Deuteronomy's lament that the LORD had 'not given a heart to know, eyes to see' supplies the unbelief-as-imposed-blindness motif Paul fuses with Isaiah. Paul cites this very verse in Rom 11:8, raising its availability and coherence here.

echoes.text: to open the blind eyes, to bring the prisoners out of the dungeon, and those who sit in darkness out of the prison.
echoes.note: The Servant's task to 'open blind eyes' frames Paul's gospel as the light that should dawn; 42:19's 'blind servant' sharpens the irony of unbelieving blindness. Volume is moderate but coherence with the Isaianic light/blindness cluster Paul is mining is strong.

echoes.text: For she is an effulgence from everlasting light, And an unspotted mirror of the working of God, And an image of his goodness.
echoes.note: Wisdom as 'image of his goodness' and radiance of glory is the Second-Temple lexicon for Christ as 'image of God' and 'glory of Christ.' Availability and coherence are high; volume rests on shared eikon/glory vocabulary rather than a quotation.

echoes.text: For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of Yahweh’s glory, as the waters cover the sea.
echoes.note: 'The light of the knowledge of the glory of God' closely tracks Habakkuk's promise that the earth will be filled with 'the knowledge of the glory of the LORD.' The triple chain knowledge-glory-LORD is distinctive enough to register as more than coincidence.

echoes.text: The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light. Those who lived in the land of the shadow of death, on them the light has shined.
echoes.note: Light shining on those in darkness echoes Isaiah's people who 'walked in darkness' seeing a great light, reinforcing the gospel-as-dawn imagery. Coherent with the Isaianic light theme already in play, though the verbal contact is general.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
echoes.note: 'The glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ' continues ch. 3's contrast with the glory on Moses' face, transferring the shining-face motif to Christ. Recurrence from the immediately prior argument makes the Exodus glory narrative the controlling subtext.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh’s glory settled on Mount Sinai, and the cloud covered it six days. The seventh day he called to Moses out of the midst of the cloud.
echoes.note: The Sinai theophany supplies Mark's frame: the glory of the LORD settled on the mountain, the cloud covered it six days, and on the seventh day God called to Moses out of the cloud. Mark's 'after six days,' the high mountain, the overshadowing cloud, and the voice from the cloud reproduce this cluster with high volume and tight coherence. The Transfiguration is staged as a new Sinai.

echoes.text: Moses went up on the mountain, and the cloud covered the mountain.
echoes.note: Moses goes up the mountain and the cloud covers it, the immediate setting for the giving of the covenant. Mark's ascent of three named companions onto a high mountain into a cloud reactivates this Sinai ascent. The recurrence of mountain-and-cloud theophany makes the availability and coherence criteria strong.

echoes.text: When Moses came down from Mount Sinai with the two tablets of the testimony in Moses’ hand, when he came down from the mountain, Moses didn’t know that the skin of his face shone by reason of his speaking with him.
echoes.note: When Moses came down from Sinai the skin of his face shone because he had talked with God, so that the people were afraid. Jesus' garments becoming dazzling white and the disciples' fear echo the transfigured radiance of Moses, while transposing the glory from reflected to inherent. The Moses-glory pattern is reinforced by Moses' actual presence on the mountain.

echoes.text: I will tell of the decree. Yahweh said to me, “You are my son. Today I have become your father.
echoes.note: The heavenly voice 'This is my beloved Son' draws on the royal-enthronement decree 'You are my Son.' The divine sonship language frames Jesus as the messianic king. Recurrence of Psalm 2 at the baptism (Mark 1:11) and here establishes a Markan inclusio of divine attestation.

echoes.text: Yahweh your God will raise up to you a prophet from your midst, of your brothers, like me. You shall listen to him.
echoes.note: Moses promises a prophet like himself whom God will raise up, and commands 'to him you shall listen.' The heavenly 'Listen to him' verbally echoes this command, and the presence of Moses on the mountain makes the prophet-like-Moses identification pointed. Volume and coherence are both strong.

echoes.text: Yahweh descended in the cloud, and stood with him there, and proclaimed Yahweh’s name.
echoes.note: The LORD descended in the cloud and stood with Moses and proclaimed his name. The descending cloud and the divine voice in Mark cohere with this Sinai descent, reinforcing the Moses typology already active through Moses' appearance.

echoes.text: “Behold, my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen, in whom my soul delights— I have put my Spirit on him. He will bring justice to the nations.
echoes.note: 'Behold my servant, my chosen, in whom my soul delights' stands behind the beloved-Son acclamation, blending servant election with sonship. The Markan voice fuses Psalm 2 royal sonship with Isaianic servant language. The servant motif coheres with the suffering Son of Man that immediately follows.

echoes.text: He said, “Now take your son, your only son, whom you love, even Isaac, and go into the land of Moriah. Offer him there for a burnt offering on one of the mountains which I will tell you of.”
echoes.note: God's command to Abraham regarding 'your son, your only son, whom you love' supplies the Aqedah resonance behind 'my beloved Son.' The Greek agapetos echoes the Septuagint of Isaac, linking divine sonship to sacrificial offering, which coheres with Mark's passion theme. The connection is suggestive rather than verbally exact.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: Elijah's appearance on the mountain activates the expectation that Elijah will come before the day of the LORD, made explicit in 9:11-13. His presence beside Moses pairs Law and Prophets as witnesses to Jesus. The motif is developed verbally in the following pericope.

echoes.text: As they still went on, and talked, behold, a chariot of fire and horses of fire separated them; and Elijah went up by a whirlwind into heaven.
echoes.note: Elijah's being taken up to heaven by chariot explains why he, like Moses (whose death and burial were hidden), is available to appear on the mountain rather than being among the dead. The translation traditions of both figures underwrite their eschatological reappearance. Coherence with Jewish expectation is strong though the verbal contact is nil.

echoes.text: I saw until thrones were placed, and one who was ancient of days sat: his clothing was white as snow, and the hair of his head like pure wool; his throne was fiery flames, and its wheels burning fire.
echoes.note: The clothing white as snow in Daniel's vision of the Ancient of Days lies behind Mark's description of garments dazzling white beyond any launderer's whitening. The apocalyptic-glory vocabulary transfers heavenly radiance onto Jesus. Volume is moderate and coheres with Mark's son-of-man Christology.

echoes.text: “Behold, I send my messenger, and he will prepare the way before me; and the Lord, whom you seek, will suddenly come to his temple; and the messenger of the covenant, whom you desire, behold, he comes!” says Yahweh of Armies.
echoes.note: The messenger sent to prepare the way contributes to the Elijah-forerunner complex evoked by Elijah's presence. The link here is indirect, mediated through Mark's broader Elijah typology.

echoes.text: So Moses the servant of Yahweh died there in the land of Moab, according to Yahweh’s word.
echoes.note: Moses' death on Mount Nebo with no known grave fed traditions of his assumption, making his appearance alongside Elijah intelligible. The faint link supports the availability of Moses as a heavenly witness. It rests on later interpretive tradition rather than the text alone.

echoes.text: As Aaron spoke to the whole congregation of the children of Israel, they looked toward the wilderness, and behold, Yahweh’s glory appeared in the cloud.
echoes.note: The glory of the LORD appearing in the cloud in the wilderness contributes to the cloud-glory motif overshadowing the disciples. The general theophanic cloud is shared, though Exodus 24 is the primary source. A faint reinforcing echo.

echoes.text: You shall dwell in booths seven days. All who are native-born in Israel shall dwell in booths,
echoes.note: Peter's proposal to make three booths (skenai) may draw on the Feast of Booths command to dwell in temporary shelters, evoking eschatological feast and divine dwelling. The link is contested and may be incidental to Peter's confusion. If intended, it ties the theophany to Sukkot's hope of God's tabernacling presence.

echoes.text: It will happen that everyone who is left of all the nations that came against Jerusalem will go up from year to year to worship the King, Yahweh of Armies, and to keep the feast of tents.
echoes.note: Zechariah's vision of all nations keeping the Feast of Booths when the LORD becomes king supplies a possible eschatological-Sukkot backdrop to Peter's tents. The connection is faint and depends on reading the booths motif eschatologically. It coheres with the kingdom-with-power saying of 9:1.

echoes.text: Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of Yahweh comes.
echoes.note: The scribal teaching that 'Elijah must come first' directly reflects Malachi's promise to send Elijah before the great and terrible day of the LORD. Jesus affirms and reinterprets this expectation, identifying the returned Elijah with John the Baptist. Verbal and thematic volume is high.

echoes.text: He will turn the hearts of the fathers to the children, and the hearts of the children to their fathers, lest I come and strike the earth with a curse.”
echoes.note: Elijah's task to 'turn the hearts' and so restore relationships underlies Jesus' phrase that Elijah 'restores all things.' The restoration motif is drawn directly from Malachi's commission. Coherence with the forerunner role is exact.

echoes.text: Who was recorded for reproofs in their seasons, To pacify anger, before it brake forth into wrath; To turn the heart of the father to the son, And to restore the tribes of Jacob.
echoes.note: Sirach interprets Malachi, saying Elijah is ready to calm wrath, turn the heart of the father to the son, and restore the tribes of Jacob. Jesus' wording that Elijah 'restores all things' tracks Sirach's restorationist gloss more closely than Malachi alone, demonstrating Second-Temple availability. This is a key deuterocanonical witness to the expectation Mark engages.

echoes.text: He was despised, and rejected by men; a man of suffering, and acquainted with disease. He was despised as one from whom men hide their face; and we didn’t respect him.
echoes.note: Jesus' question 'how is it written about the Son of Man, that he should suffer many things and be despised' draws on the servant who is despised and rejected by men. The suffering-and-despised pairing matches Isaiah's fourth servant song closely. Mark grounds the passion in this Scripture as 'written.'

echoes.text: Surely he has borne our sickness, and carried our suffering; yet we considered him plagued, struck by God, and afflicted.
echoes.note: The servant who bears griefs and is esteemed stricken reinforces the 'suffer many things' clause. The vicarious-suffering theme coheres with Mark's repeated passion predictions. Volume is moderate alongside the stronger 53:3 contact.

echoes.text: But I am a worm, and no man; a reproach of men, and despised by the people.
echoes.note: The sufferer 'despised by the people' supplies a scriptural template for the Son of Man being 'despised.' Mark's passion narrative repeatedly draws on Psalm 22, making its recurrence a strong coherence indicator. The verbal contact on contempt strengthens the echo.

echoes.text: Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
echoes.note: Jezebel's threat to kill Elijah, who flees for his life, stands behind 'they have also done to him whatever they wanted,' applied to John the Baptist's persecution and death. The historical Elijah's suffering at royal hands prefigures the returned Elijah's fate. Coherence with the rejected-prophet pattern is strong.

echoes.text: I saw in the night visions, and behold, there came with the clouds of the sky one like a son of man, and he came even to the ancient of days, and they brought him near before him.
echoes.note: The title 'Son of Man,' twice used in this pericope, derives from Daniel's heavenly figure, here paradoxically joined to suffering. Mark fuses Danielic exaltation with Isaianic suffering. The recurrence of the title throughout Mark anchors the Danielic source.

echoes.text: He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and slain your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
echoes.note: Elijah's lament that the Israelites have killed the prophets and seek his life reinforces the pattern that the forerunner suffers as the prophets did. The link to 'done to him whatever they wanted' is thematic. It supports reading John's death through an Elijah lens.

echoes.text: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner.
echoes.note: The rejected stone supplies a scriptural pattern of the chosen one being despised and rejected, coherent with the Son of Man being 'set at nought.' Mark cites this psalm later (12:10), making its availability and recurrence plausible. The contact here is faint.

harmony.title: The Transfiguration
harmony.note: Moses and Elijah, the bright cloud, the voice — "This is my beloved Son." John, who was there, never tells it.

doctrine.title: Nicene Creed
doctrine.article: God from God, Light from Light

registers.label: Spare
lines: They climbed the mountain and saw him changed.
His clothes a dazzling white, no bleach so bright.
A cloud overshadowed them, and a voice spoke.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
The God who said: let light shine out of darkness,
has shone in our hearts with the glory of Christ.
Come, let us worship on the holy mountain.
Listen to him, the Beloved. Amen.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: They went up the high mountain, just the three of them, and there before their eyes he was transfigured, his clothes blazing whiter than anything on earth.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
Moses and Elijah stood with him, and Peter, hardly knowing what to say, blurted out: Lord, it is good for us to be here.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
Then a cloud came down and wrapped them in shadow, and out of the cloud a voice spoke that silenced every other.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
The God who said, Let light shine out of darkness, has lit our hearts with the face of Christ. Come and behold him.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him! Amen.

registers.label: Hybrid
lines: They climb the mountain and see him blaze with light.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
A cloud comes down, and a voice speaks from it.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
Light shines out of darkness into our hearts.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him!
Come, let us worship on the holy mountain.
This is my Son, the Beloved; listen to him! Amen.
